lines: Human Rights Watch monitors human rights abuses in about 90 countries worldwide. We've been working on the worst forms of child labor for over 20 years. So for example, we have looked at child labor in sugarcane plantations in El Salvador, banana plantations in Ecuador, cotton farming in Egypt, the silk industry in India, as well as others.

For the last three years, we've been focused on child labor in tobacco farming. Previously, we have investigated tobacco farming as well in the United States and in Brazil. But today, we're here to talk to you about our new report on child labor and tobacco farming here in Indonesia.

[Music] We started our investigation on hazardous child labor and tobacco farming in Indonesia in September of 2014. Over the course of two growing seasons, 2014 and 2015, we interviewed 132 children who worked on tobacco farms. These children were between the ages of 8 and 17. And they worked on tobacco farms in four Indonesian provinces, East

Java, Central Java, West Java, and West Nusa, Lombok Island. Almost 3/4 of the children we interviewed had started working in tobacco farming by the time they were 12. And they worked on farms that were operated by their families, by their neighbors, and by other farmers in their communities. Tobacco in any form contains nicotine. And when workers are

handling tobacco, they can absorb this nicotine through their skin and it can cause acute nicotine poisoning. The most common symptoms of acute nicotine poisoning are nausea, vomiting, headaches, and dizziness. And half of the children we interviewed in Indonesia experienced one or more of these symptoms while they worked in tobacco farming. Many children also handled and mixed very toxic chemicals, pesticides,

and fertilizers. And a number of these children reported immediate illness after working around these chemicals. So some of them would mix the chemicals themselves. Some of them would spray the fields with tanks and other children worked in fields while adult workers sprayed chemicals nearby. These children

often reported headaches, dizziness, stomach pains, difficulty breathing, coughing, and sneezing, and other effects when they were working around these toxic chemicals. The long-term effects of pesticide exposure for children whose bodies and brains are still developing include cancer,

problems with reproductive health, problems with learning, and other issues. Children are particularly vulnerable to the harmful effects of toxins like nicotine and pesticides. Their bodies and brains continue developing you know through the teenage years and brain development continues into the early 20s. Uh, children also are smaller in

size and have more years of their life left to develop chronic health effects from working in close proximity with these toxins. Many children we interviewed also suffered pain and fatigue from lifting heavy loads or engaging in the same motions repeatedly for hours on end, twisting their wrists,

lifting things above their heads. And they talked about having pain in their backs and their necks and their wrists and other parts of their body. Some children also used sharp tools and cut themselves or climbed into the rafters of barns to hang tobacco to dry with nothing to protect them from falling.

Some children also talked about feeling lightheaded or dizzy while working on extremely hot days and in high heat and full sun. And a few children actually collapsed and fainted in the fields while working in the heat. Most of the children and the parents that we interviewed had never received

comprehensive information and training about the dangers to children of work in tobacco farming. Most of the children we interviewed attended school and worked primarily before and after school on weekends and school holidays. But there were some children who dropped out of school early to work to help support

their families. And some children who missed many days of school in a row during the harvest season because they said they needed to work to help their families. The tobacco that these children help to produce is purchased by both large Indonesian tobacco companies as well as some of the largest multinational tobacco companies in the world. None of these companies are doing enough to make sure that the tobacco

that they produce or that they purchase is not produced with hazardous child labor. In Indonesia, the five largest tobacco companies or purchasers include three Indonesian companies and two multinationals. The Indonesian companies are Jarum, Gurum Goram and Noy Rono. And then two uh other companies, Bentel is

owned by British American Tobacco and Sora is owned by Philip Morris International. And other Indonesian and multinationals purchase tobacco here as well. Several months ago, human wrote, Human Rights Watch wrote to 13 companies to share our findings from our research. 10 of the 13 responded. Jarum and Guram Gurum did not respond at all despite repeated attempts to reach them. We

asked them about their policies and practices regarding child labor. The two multinational companies responded and detailed some action they are taking. In Indonesia, tobacco is purchased through diff two different methods. The most common is the open market system. So, a local farmer will sell his tobacco to a local trader. That trader may sell it to another trader and then to a

warehouse that's owned by one of the tobacco companies. In that open market system, none of the companies buying the tobacco can say exactly where it comes from. Yeah. [Music] Some companies, especially the multinational companies, have direct contacts contracts with the farmer. So, they're buying the the tobacco directly

from the farm where it's produced. So, they have a much better chance of finding um you know whether or not child labor is a problem. But we found child labor in both situations and all of the companies purchase at least some of their tobacco through the open market system. So in our report, we're making recommendations to both the companies and to the government. To the companies,

we're urging them to adopt or strengthen child labor policies to prohibit any hazardous child labor for children under the age of 18. and that includes any direct contact with tobacco in any form. We're also urging them to only buy tobacco from suppliers that enforce this policy. The Indonesian government's

child labor policies or child labor laws are good ones. They are in line with international standards. They prohibit child labor before the age of 15, except for light work by children between 13 and 15. and they prohibit hazardous child labor before the age of 18. But we see three particular gaps. First of all, the existing law is not well enforced.

Indonesia only has 2,000 labor inspectors for the entire country and they do not inspect conditions on the small family farms where tobacco is produced. A second gap is even though Indonesia has prohibited hazardous labor for children under the age of 18, the list that of hazardous tasks that it has issued is a bit ambiguous. It says that

children should not work with harmful chemical substances, but it has not made clear that nicotine and exposure to tobacco leaves is included. So, another thing we're asking the Indonesian government to do is to revise its list or issue a new regulation or or decree making clear that nicotine and exposure to nicotine is a harmful chemical substance that is considered prohibited.

And then the third uh gap is public education. So, we're asking the government to conduct a massive ed public education campaign to make sure that tobacco farming families fully understand the threats to the health of their children from exposure to nicotine and these pesticides. So, within the next few weeks, the tobacco season is going to get underway in Indonesia again

and thousands of children, possibly tens of thousands of children will being will be going back into the tobacco fields to work. So, we feel some urgency and are urging both tobacco companies and the Indonesian government to act swiftly to protect these children from hazardous child labor and tobacco farming. So, thank you very much for coming today.
